author: Gregory Thaumaturgus
occasion: The surviving fragment contrasts the honor given to the God who truly exists with the honor given to a god who does not exist, stating the opposite effects each has on the one who gives honor.
argument: Honor directed toward the God who truly exists is itself an honor to the one who gives it. By contrast, honor directed toward a god who does not exist is, from the opposite direction, dishonor to the one who gives it. The fragment thus distinguishes two kinds of honor based on whether their object truly exists, and states that each kind rebounds on the worshiper accordingly.

outline.move: The author states that honoring the truly existing God honors the one who honors, while honoring a nonexistent god is, from the opposite direction, dishonor to the one who honors.

uncertain: The original extent and structure of the work are unknown because only this fragment survives.
The date of composition cannot be established from the fragment.
The addressee or original audience cannot be determined from the surviving text.
Whether the work explicitly discussed idols or idolatry cannot be established from this fragment, since the terms εἰδωλολατρεία and εἴδωλον do not occur in the surviving text.

_unresolved_facts.claim: The surviving fragment contrasts the honor given to the God who truly exists with the honor given to a god who does not exist, stating the opposite effects each has on the one who gives honor.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ἡ δὲ εἰς τὸν οὐκ ὄντα θεὸν τιμὴ ἐξ ἐναντίας αὐτοῦ τοῦ τιμῶντός ἐστιν ἀτιμία
_unresolved_facts.fix: The surviving fragment contrasts honor given to the God who truly exists with honor given to 'the non-existent' (τὸν οὐκ ὄντα), not specifically 'a god who does not exist.' The text uses τὸν οὐκ ὄντα without θεόν as predicate: the second instance refers back to θεόν from the first clause, but the phrasing is 'the one who is not' rather than 'a god who does not exist.'

_unresolved_facts.claim: Honor directed toward a god who does not exist is, from the opposite direction, dishonor to the one who gives it.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ἡ δὲ εἰς τὸν οὐκ ὄντα θεὸν τιμὴ ἐξ ἐναντίας αὐτοῦ τοῦ τιμῶντός ἐστιν ἀτιμία
_unresolved_facts.fix: Honor directed toward the non-existent (τὸν οὐκ ὄντα) is, from the opposite direction, dishonor to the one who honors (αὐτοῦ τοῦ τιμῶντός). The brief's 'gives it' adds words not in the source; the Greek simply says 'the one who honors.'

_unresolved_facts.claim: The fragment thus distinguishes two kinds of honor based on whether their object truly exists, and states that each kind rebounds on the worshiper accordingly.
_unresolved_facts.fix: The fragment does not use the concept of 'rebounding' or describe a mechanism of return; it simply states a static equivalence (ἐστιν) in each case. 'Rebounds' and 'accordingly' impose a causal or dynamic framework not explicit in the Greek.

_unresolved_facts.claim: The author states that honoring the truly existing God honors the one who honors, while honoring a nonexistent god is, from the opposite direction, dishonor to the one who honors.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ἡ μὲν εἰς θεὸν τὸν ὄντως ὄντα τιμὴ πάντως που καὶ αὐτοῦ τοῦ τιμῶντός ἐστι τιμή
_unresolved_facts.fix: The author states that honoring the God who truly exists is 'undoubtedly also' (πάντως που καὶ) honor to the one who honors—not simply 'honors the one who honors.' The πάντως που ('undoubtedly,' 'assuredly') and καί ('also') are omitted, weakening the epistemic force and the sense that this is an additional benefit.
